question: The Saf-Ski of 1937 pioneered toe release in these devices, letting go when twisting force passed a set limit. Around 1972 a Teflon anti-friction pad began to be fitted to them, and injury rates in alpine skiing started to fall. Modern alpine versions have a toe piece, a heel piece and a brake that stops a ski running away when they release. They are set to a DIN number that depends on the skier's weight, height and ability. For 10 points, name these devices that hold a boot to a ski and, on alpine skis, release it in a fall.

This area's lifts include three cable cars, 37 gondolas and 69 chairlifts, and it claims to be the largest fully connected ski area in the world. It was interconnected in 1971, and its resort La Tania was developed for the 1992 Albertville Winter Olympics. The village of Orelle, on the Maurienne side, was joined to it by a gondola between 1995 and 1997 and holds its highest point, at 3,230 metres. It lies in Savoie, in the Tarentaise, and partly within Vanoise National Park. For 10 points, name this French ski area of about 600 km of slopes that links Courchevel, Méribel, Val Thorens and Les Menuires.
answer: Les Trois Vallées [or Les 3 Vallées or Three Valleys or Trois Vallees or 3 Vallees]

question: This resort has eleven villages, and its lowest, Montchavin, sits at 1,250 metres while its highest point is the Glacier de la Chiaupe at 3,250 metres. It opened on 24 December 1961 with two drag lifts and four slopes, and a second village followed in 1969. Its bobsleigh, luge and skeleton track was built for the 1992 Albertville Winter Olympics and is due to be reused in 2030. In 2014 it was named the most popular ski resort in the world, with over 2.5 million visitors a season, and it has 225 km of slopes. For 10 points, name this French resort in Savoie which since 2003 has been linked to Les Arcs by the Vanoise Express, forming Paradiski.
answer: La Plagne [or Plagne; prompt on "Paradiski"; do not accept "Les Arcs"]

question: Its first product, the BB1, was inspired by a 1965 toy called the Snurfer and had a single strap, with a rope and handle on the nose. It was founded in 1977 in Londonderry, Vermont, where its boards were first made by hand in a garage, and it moved to Manchester, Vermont in 1978 and later to Burlington. Its founder campaigned to open lifts to snowboarders, and in 1982 Suicide Six became the first mountain to admit them. In 1985 it established the U.S. Open Snowboarding Championships, and by the 2010s it held 40 to 45 percent of the snowboard market. For 10 points, name this Vermont snowboard maker, named for the middle name of its late founder Jake Carpenter.

This mishap is a main reason why learning the sport has a reputation for being painful. It can happen on the toe side or the heel side of the board, and it is the sideways part of a rider's velocity that causes it. The steel rim on the downhill side of the board digs into the snow while the rider's body keeps moving forward, rotating them down and throwing them at the ground. Novices typically suffer it many times before they master carving turns. For 10 points, give this three-word phrase for the beginner's fall in which the downhill rim of a snowboard snags the snow.
answer: catching an edge [or catch an edge or caught an edge or catches an edge or catch edge or catching edges; prompt on "edge" or "falling" or "crashing"]

question: It was established in 1965 by Maurice Herzog, the French mountaineer who led the 1950 expedition to Annapurna. It is a non-profit association whose members include government bodies, sports federations and youth associations, and it is headquartered in Paris. It has a presence in about fifty countries, and about 250,000 people travel with it every year. It generally serves ages 18 to 45, though its advanced and expert courses take participants up to 55, and it also runs vocational training for sports careers. For 10 points, give the four-letter acronym of this French organisation that runs budget sports holidays, including group ski trips for young adults.
answer: UCPA [or Union nationale des centres sportifs de plein air]

question: A version of this device that detaches from its cable was introduced by a French lift manufacturer, whose name is often used for it. Traditional ones run at up to 3.0 m/s, while detachable ones run at about 4 m/s, and they suit the low-capacity needs of beginner slopes. Unlike a rope tow, it needs no grip strength, and unlike a T-bar it uses a disc rather than a shaped bar. The disc is placed between a skier's legs so that they are pulled uphill while staying on the snow, whereas snowboarders hold it in position with their hands. For 10 points, name this surface lift, named for the small plastic disc that tows riders up a beginner slope.
answer: button lift [or platter lift or drag lift or Poma lift or Poma; prompt on "surface lift"; do not accept "T-bar" or "rope tow"]

question: The Kohlerer Bahn in Bolzano, opened in 1908, is described as the first modern enclosed aerial lift built solely for passengers. Its cabins are connected to a continuously circulating cable by spring-loaded grips, which let them slow down and detach in the stations. Monocable, bicable and tricable versions exist, and the bicable type is more stable in wind. Medellín's Metrocable and La Paz's Mi Teleférico use this kind of system as public transport. For 10 points, name this kind of ski-resort lift with enclosed cabins, unlike a chairlift, which shares its name with a boat of Venice.
answer: gondola [or gondola lift or gondolas; prompt on "aerial lift" or "cable car"; do not accept "chairlift"]

question: Although the word for skiing itself comes from Old Norse by way of Norwegian, this custom has a French name. The name was chosen because of the early popularity of such activities in the French Alps. It is most popular in Alpine regions, though it has spread to ski destinations all over the world. Skiers often stop at bars on their last run of the day while still wearing all of their ski gear. For 10 points, give this French term for the drinking, dancing and other nightlife at a ski resort once the lifts have closed.
answer: après-ski [or apres ski or apres-ski or après ski or apres; prompt on "nightlife"]

question: These were adapted from workwear that emerged in the 1890s through Levi Strauss & Co. and became common among farmers, miners, loggers and railroad workers during the Great Depression. That original garment was usually made of denim, though corduroy, chino cloth or leather were also used. The adapted versions are made of wind- and waterproof fabric and have adjustable shoulder braces. In British English the original garment is called dungarees, but this is a French word. For 10 points, give this French-derived term for bib-and-brace trousers worn for skiing, sailing and diving.
answer: salopettes [or salopette; prompt on "ski pants" or "bib pants" or "dungarees" or "overalls"]

question: This substance is applied to the base of skis, snowboards and toboggans to adjust their coefficient of friction for the snow conditions of the day. Cross-country classic skiers use a variant of it, sometimes called kick wax, to grip the snow during their forward stride, choosing a hard formulation for fresh snow and a sticky klister for old or wet snow. Its other main form, used by both alpine and cross-country skiers, instead minimizes sliding friction and has historically been made from paraffin, later joined by fluorocarbons and graphite. Applying it also fills in scratches and gouges that rocks and ice leave in a ski's base. For 10 points, name this substance skiers and snowboarders melt or rub onto their equipment's underside.

Founded in 1947 in Annecy in a one-room metalworking shop, this company began by making steel ski edges before founder François's son Georges took the reins. Its 1957 Skade toe piece transformed ski bindings, helping it become the world's leading binding manufacturer by 1972. It later branched into footwear with the 1979 SX90 boot and into cross-country gear with the 1980 SNS system. Adidas bought the company in 1997 before selling it to Amer Sports in 2005. For 10 points, name this French sporting-goods company, a major maker of ski bindings, boots and boards.

Created in 1974, this ski-area consortium spans roughly 3,000 square kilometres of northeastern Italy and unites twelve separate resorts under one lift pass. Around 97 percent of its 1,246 kilometres of slopes are covered by snowmaking, guaranteeing skiing from December to April even without fresh snowfall. Its 450 lifts make it, by total piste length, the largest ski area in the world, spanning the limestone peaks of the Dolomites. For 10 points, give the name of this Italian ski pass and area, whose name literally means "super ski" in Italian.

A former ski instructor named Luc Reversade founded this on-mountain establishment in Val d'Isère in 1974 with his mother and a chef named Mamone, after visiting party spots in Ibiza, Turkey and Miami for inspiration. Its 1980 addition of an open-air bar, paired with live music and elaborately costumed dancers performing on tabletops, turned it into a full-blown daytime clubbing experience. Its original Val d'Isère outpost sits at 2,400 metres, and the concept has since expanded to Val Thorens, Méribel, Les Arcs and Alpe d'Huez. For 10 points, name this chain of raucous French mountainside restaurant-bars whose name translates to "the sweet madness."

This city's airport, established in 1919 and given a terminal building in 1946, has an unusual bi-national layout that lets arriving passengers walk directly into either of two countries. It handled nearly 17.8 million passengers in 2024 and serves as the busiest air gateway to the Portes du Soleil, the Mont Blanc massif and the Tarentaise Valley's ski resorts. Straddling the Swiss-French border, it is the closest major airport to Chamonix, Verbier and Morzine. For 10 points, name this Swiss city on its namesake lake, headquarters to numerous international organizations.

Standing at an official height of 4,807 metres, this peak on the French-Italian border was first summited on 8 August 1786 by Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat, an ascent often called the birth of mountaineering. It towers just south of the resort town of Chamonix and is nicknamed the Roof of Europe. For 10 points, name this highest peak in the Alps and in Western Europe, whose French name literally means "white mountain."

This portmanteau term describes snow produced when cold air masses from Siberia cross the Sea of Japan, pick up moisture, and are forced upward by Japan's mountain ranges, cooling rapidly into exceptionally light, dry flakes. Riders sometimes call the month of peak conditions for it "Japanuary." It is especially prized in Hokkaido, where resorts advertise its high volume and fine, dry texture as superior to typical Alpine or North American snow. For 10 points, give this slang blend of a country's name with a word for fresh, fluffy snow.

This ski area occupies a single mountain in Hokkaido and comprises four separately managed resorts: Grand Hirafu, Hanazono, Niseko Village and Annupuri. Hokkaido's first unified lift-ticket system, the Free Passport, launched here in November 1993, and by 1998 it had grown into an All Mountain Pass covering every lift across all four areas. Tokyu Land Corporation has controlled Grand Hirafu since 2004, while a Hong Kong real-estate firm has run Hanazono since 2007, yet skiers can move seamlessly across shared terrain linking every resort. For 10 points, name this Hokkaido ski area, famed among powder-hunters for its Japow, whose four resorts share a name with the surrounding town.

This valley's Happo-One resort hosted the men's downhill, super-G and combined alpine skiing events, along with ski jumping, at the 1998 Winter Olympics. Today it comprises ten interconnected resorts served by 92 lifts and 137 runs stretched across some 30 kilometres, and it receives over 11 metres of snowfall a year. It lies in the same prefecture that hosted those 1998 Games. For 10 points, name this Japanese ski valley, home to the Happo-One resort.

Australians Matthew Hampton and Mick Klima founded this ski and snowboard rental and retail company in 2005, eventually opening seven stores across Niseko, Hakuba and Furano. In 2022 it was acquired in full by the American outdoor retailer Evo, after which Hampton joined Evo's leadership team as managing director for the Asia-Pacific region. It equips travelers who arrive without their own gear to chase Japan's famous powder snow. For 10 points, name this Japan-based ski and snowboard rental chain, whose name is also a word for a regular, repeated pattern in music.
